bc25d513037e854e.text: {"thought": "The time step test fails at an adjustment time of 0.5 weeks for both weights tried; the other tests passed in every run.", "answer": "One test fails: the time step. With inventory_adjustment_time 0.5 weeks, halving dt from 0.125 to 0.0625 changes the factory's amplification by 5.4% (17.13 to 16.26) at supply_line_weight 0.25, and by 6.6% (9.5 to 8.91) at weight 1. At the chapter's 2 weeks the change is 2.0%. No inventory went below zero (lowest 58.7 and 59.0 cases), the floor never acted and the goods gap stayed at or below 2.7e-12 cases, even with step_size 1, no supply line weight and a 0.5-week adjustment time. The failure is numerical, not structural: use a smaller dt when adjustment times are short."}

899832534be44f5f.text: The swings at the factory are made inside the chain, not by customers: with demand that varies week to week, factory orders varied 5.6 times as much as sales, and at times fell to zero. Counting open orders, sharing shop sales data and halving delivery times each help; together they cut the factory's swing to 1.2 times that of sales and the chain's cost by 18 a week. If only one is possible, share sales data: its worst factory ratio across nine behavioural scenarios is 5.1, against 13.7 as found, but in a lasting 30% surge it raises backlog costs from about 2,460 to 3,650 unless stages also count open orders. With all three measures, factory orders will hold between 77 and 124 cases a week, so the factory can plan steady production.
